Have you ever found yourself wrestling with questions about faith, or wondered where the divine fits into our most personal struggles? If so, you’re not alone—and you’re in good company. Welcome to a journey where the world of psychological healing gently intertwines with the mystery of spiritual experience. Together, we’ll explore what happens when pain, doubt, and transformation lead us to search for meaning and connection—sometimes stumbling right into something greater than ourselves. Through the compassionate lens of Ara C. Trembly, MS MA LPC, in his book The Right Hand of God: A Psychotherapist's Case for the Reality of the Living God, we’ll discover how the boundaries between science and spirituality begin to blur, and how the longing for the sacred weaves into the complexities of the mind.
Along the way, you’ll hear personal stories and clinical moments that shine a light on how belief in a living God can shape the journey of recovery and growth. We’ll move together through crisis, hope, and those quiet revelations that suggest maybe the presence of the divine isn’t just a matter of doctrine—but something real you can witness and feel, even in the midst of a therapeutic conversation.
As we peel back the layers of distress, you’ll see that healing might not just be about techniques or theories—it could also be about grace. So, let’s walk this path together, and open ourselves to the possibility that the right hand of God is reaching out, even in our moments of deepest need. Here’s to discovering what it truly means to be whole—mind, heart, and spirit.

Chapter 1: Searching for Something Real—The Longing for God in Everyday Life
Have you ever felt that quiet ache, that subtle sense that something’s missing—even when, on the outside, your life looks just fine?
Maybe it’s a restlessness that sneaks up in the middle of a busy day, or an emptiness that lingers after you hit a milestone and still don’t feel fulfilled. Sometimes, it’s a sharper longing—a deep ache that surfaces when life falls apart and nothing the world offers seems to satisfy.
That longing, even when we can’t quite name it, is where so many journeys begin—a journey that brings together faith, doubt, and the search for meaning.
In therapy, this ache shows up in all kinds of ways. Imagine a woman sitting across from her counselor, nervously twisting her hands as she tries to put words to a sadness that just won’t go away. She’s read the books, tried meditation, even turned to medication, but that heaviness still lingers. Or picture a young man who, on paper, seems to have it all together—but deep down, he feels like a fraud, haunted by the sense that his life is missing something essential.
These stories aren’t rare. If you listen closely, you’ll hear the same quiet questions echoing in countless hearts: Is there more to life than what I see? Does anyone really care? Is God out there, and if so, could He possibly care about me?
Now, for those who grew up around religion, these questions can feel even heavier. Maybe you remember praying as a kid and feeling like nobody answered. Or maybe you sat through church services that left you cold, or got burned by hypocrisy or judgment, making you want to steer clear of anything religious. But even among the skeptics, there’s often a longing for something beyond what we can touch or measure. It’s almost as if our hearts are wired to reach for the divine—even when our minds want to push it away.
In the therapy room, these aren’t just big, abstract questions—they’re deeply personal. Picture a dad, struggling with anxiety, who admits he sometimes whispers prayers when no one’s around, not sure if anyone’s even listening. Or a college student, weighed down by depression, asking if God could possibly care about someone as broken as she feels. These moments are raw and honest, and they reveal something important: beneath the pain we carry, there’s often a spiritual hunger that’s just waiting to be named.
It’s tempting to write off these longings as wishful thinking, or just the result of how we were raised. And, honestly, a lot of folks in mental health have been taught to be skeptical of spiritual experiences—sometimes seeing them as nothing more than coping mechanisms or even warning signs.
But after years of listening to people’s stories, a different picture starts to emerge. Again and again, people describe moments they can’t explain—encounters with something, or Someone, that feels loving, powerful, and unmistakably real. Sometimes it’s a breakthrough in the middle of a crisis; other times, it’s a gentle reassurance that slips quietly into an ordinary day.
Like the woman grieving her child, who talks about a deep peace that washed over her one night. She can’t put words to it, but she knows it was real. Or the man fighting addiction, who suddenly finds a strength he never knew he had. These aren’t rare, dramatic stories—they’re woven through everyday life, often hidden behind layers of doubt or shame.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: this longing for God isn’t a flaw or an illusion. It’s a core part of being human—a sign that we’re made for something more. Healing, then, isn’t just about fixing symptoms or changing habits. It’s about being open to the idea that the ache inside might be pointing toward something real. Maybe even Someone who’s closer than we ever thought possible.

Chapter 2: When Faith and Therapy Meet—Integrating Spirituality and Psychology.
You know, for years, psychology and faith seemed to exist in totally separate worlds. Therapists focused on the mind and emotions, while spiritual leaders tended to the soul. But when real people walk through the door, those lines blur in ways that can’t be ignored. Life doesn’t fit into tidy boxes—our anxiety, our grief, our deepest pain, they always spill over into questions about hope, meaning, and even our relationship with God.
Step inside a therapist’s office, and you’ll see just how tangled these struggles can get. Imagine a woman tormented by panic attacks—her fears are all mixed up with memories of religious shame from her childhood. Or think of a man weighed down by guilt, not just craving forgiveness from those he’s hurt, but wondering if God could ever forgive him, too. These aren’t just psychological struggles; they’re spiritual wounds, and they need a different kind of care.
Some therapists feel nervous about diving into spiritual topics—they worry about crossing a line, or they’re afraid of imposing their own beliefs. Others, shaped by skepticism, might even dismiss spiritual experiences as unimportant or harmful. But what if, instead, we learned to listen more deeply? What if we honored both the science of psychology and the mystery of faith?
This kind of integration doesn’t mean forcing religious answers onto anyone, or ignoring how complex mental health can be. It’s really about making space—for honest questions, for doubt, and for exploring faith without fear of judgment. It’s about seeing that faith can be a source of strength and comfort, especially when life just feels too heavy to handle alone.
Let me share a story. One counselor remembers working with a woman raised in an ultra-strict religious home. All her life, she felt unworthy, convinced that God was angry with her. Therapy helped her see where that shame came from, but healing truly began when she started to imagine a different kind of God—a God who is compassionate, present, and loving. Through gentle conversation and prayer, she began to feel accepted in a way she’d never known before.
There’s also the story of a man struggling with addiction. His recovery wasn’t just about willpower or new habits. For him, the turning point was a growing sense of connection to something greater than himself. He described moments of surrender, like being held by a presence that gave him the courage to keep fighting. For him, faith wasn’t a crutch—it was a lifeline, a real source of hope that made change possible.
These stories aren’t rare. When people are able to weave their spiritual beliefs into their healing, something powerful happens. They find meaning in pain, hope in the struggle, and a sense of purpose that lifts them beyond their circumstances.
Of course, this process isn’t simple. Many carry deep wounds from religious communities—memories of being judged, excluded, or even abused. Others wrestle with doubt, unsure whether faith is even possible in the face of so much suffering. That’s why the therapist’s job isn’t to hand out easy answers. It’s about walking alongside, creating a safe place for honest conversation.
And in that space, something truly remarkable can happen. As people open up about their spiritual questions, they often discover that God isn’t distant or indifferent, but intimately involved in their lives. They find moments of peace, clarity, even joy—moments that don’t always make sense on paper, but feel deeply real. These experiences don’t erase pain, but they do offer a new way of seeing the world—a way rooted in the reality of a living, loving God.
So, integrating faith and therapy isn’t about picking one over the other. It’s about recognizing that real healing involves the whole person—mind, body, and spirit. And when all these parts are honored and brought together, the transformation can be deeper and more lasting than either discipline could offer alone.

Chapter 3: Encounters That Change Everything—Real Stories of Divine Presence.
You know, there are moments in life that leave a mark—experiences so powerful and unexpected, they shift the way we see the world. In therapy, these moments often sneak up on us, showing up right in the middle of ordinary conversations. But their impact? It can change everything, offering just a glimpse of something mysterious, yet deeply personal.
Picture this: one evening, a man sits alone in his living room, weighed down by years of regret. He’s made choices he wishes he could take back, and the guilt feels like a chain around his neck. He’s tried it all—apologies, self-help books, even therapy. But nothing seems to lift that heavy burden. Then, in a moment of quiet desperation, he whispers a simple prayer. He isn’t expecting anything. But suddenly, a warmth floods his chest, and for the first time in years, he feels forgiven. The memory of his mistakes is still there, but the shame? It finally loosens its grip. He can’t quite explain what happened—he just knows something real broke through.
Or take the woman who’s been battling chronic illness, feeling hopeless after doctors gave her little reason to believe things would change. The pain never lets up. One sleepless night, she senses a gentle presence in the room. It’s like a quiet reassurance, telling her she’s not alone. The pain remains, but the fear fades. Later, she describes it as being “held” by something greater than herself—a comfort that carries her through the darkest nights.
And these stories aren’t rare exceptions. Over the years, I’ve noticed a pattern: when people finally reach the end of their own strength, they often encounter a presence that feels unmistakably real. Sometimes, it’s a sudden insight—a flash of clarity that cuts through the confusion. Other times, it’s a deep, quiet peace; a sense of being truly known and loved, even when everything else feels chaotic.
One young man, gripped by anxiety, described a moment in therapy where he felt an overwhelming calm. He’d just been sharing his deepest fears, feeling completely exposed, when suddenly it was as if a heavy weight just lifted. There was no voice, no vision—just the unshakable feeling that he wasn’t alone. That moment changed everything. It gave him the courage to face his fears, and a new sense of hope he’d never had before.
Now, some people might chalk these encounters up to wishful thinking, or say it’s just emotional projection. But for those who experience them, the change is undeniable. It isn’t just a feeling—it shows up in their lives. You see new patterns of behavior, restored relationships, and a renewed sense of purpose that’s hard to ignore.
What’s really striking is how diverse these stories are. Some come from people with deep religious roots. Others? They’ve never even set foot in a church. The common thread isn’t a set of beliefs or rituals—it’s a direct encounter with something—or Someone—that brings real healing and transformation.
In the therapy room, these moments are met with respect and curiosity. Instead of rushing to explain them away, the focus is on what they mean for the person who experienced them. Often, these encounters become the bedrock for lasting change, bringing a sense of hope and direction that simple advice or technique could never offer.
Here’s what becomes clear: the presence of God isn’t limited to religious settings or special people. It shows up right in the messiness of real life—in hospital rooms, therapy offices, even in those quiet moments of desperation. These encounters don’t always fit neatly into theological boxes, but their impact is unmistakable. They’re living proof—not just of a higher power, but of a God who’s deeply involved in the details of everyday life.

Let’s talk about something truly transformative— the power of faith in healing.
We tend to picture healing as this slow, step-by-step process—something that takes time, effort, maybe the right therapy or plenty of support. But what if the real turning point isn’t about technique at all? What if it comes from a shift deep inside—from a change in what we believe is possible?
When we talk about faith here, I’m not just referring to a set of ideas or rituals. Faith is alive—it's a heartbeat, a sense of trust that God’s presence is real and active. It’s being willing to open up and actually consider that healing might not just be possible... it might already be underway.
In therapy, these shifts can be subtle, almost quiet. Picture a woman wrestling with depression. At first, she feels completely alone in her struggle. But then, she starts to pray—not out of habit, but because she’s desperate for someone to listen. Little by little, something changes. She doesn’t just feel a bit happier; she feels less isolated, more connected. The darkness doesn’t vanish overnight, but it finally begins to lift.
Or think about a man battling anger. His breakthrough doesn’t come from clenching his fists tighter, but from letting go—surrendering his pain to God. That kind of release feels risky, even foolish at first. But as he opens his hands, he finds a peace he can’t quite explain. The anger’s still there some days, but it no longer defines who he is.
These stories shine a light on something we often overlook: faith isn’t just sitting back and accepting suffering. It’s stepping into the risky business of hope—choosing to trust that something good can rise from pain. And honestly, that risk is tough. After years of disappointment, it’s easy to build walls, to protect ourselves by expecting less.
But here’s what’s remarkable. When people take that risk, even a little, things start to shift. They begin to see themselves differently. Mountains that once felt impossible to climb start to look like opportunities for growth. Broken relationships begin to mend. Even physical symptoms—chronic pain, sleepless nights, anxiety—sometimes start to ease as the mind and heart find new ground.
Now, let’s be real—faith isn’t some magic fix. Healing is still a journey, and setbacks happen. But faith changes the whole landscape. It lays down a foundation of hope, gives us a sense of purpose, and taps into strength that goes beyond what we can muster on our own.
One of the most powerful things about faith is how it reframes suffering. Instead of seeing pain as pointless, people start to find meaning in what they’re going through. Their wounds become wells of compassion and wisdom—not just for themselves, but for others, too. This shift isn’t just psychological; it’s spiritual. It’s rooted in the conviction that God is working, even when everything feels dark.
In a therapy setting, this means creating room for clients to explore what they believe, to wrestle with doubts, to hope in new ways. Sometimes that looks like prayer or meditation. Sometimes it’s just being honest about questions and fears. What matters is being open—willing to believe that healing isn’t just about what we do, but about who we trust.
And over time, the change becomes hard to ignore. People who bring faith into their healing journey often experience deeper, longer-lasting transformation. They find resilience in tough times, the courage to face their fears, and a peace that simply can’t be explained. It’s more than just a psychological boost—it’s a sign that something deeper is happening. A living God meets us in our pain... and leads us toward wholeness.

Chapter 5: Facing Doubt and Skepticism—the Challenge of Believing in a Modern World
These days, it can honestly feel like believing in God means swimming upstream. We live in a world shaped by science and skepticism, where the only things that seem to count are the ones you can measure or prove. Anything that hints at the supernatural? It's often brushed off as superstition or wishful thinking. And if you find yourself longing for something more, you might feel pretty alone—or even a little bit ashamed.
Therapy rooms aren't shielded from these pressures, either. I often see clients walk in carrying both hope and hesitation. They're not sure if their spiritual experiences will be respected, or if they'll be seen as naïve. Maybe they've been told that faith means weakness, denial, or even childishness. That kind of message can really weigh you down—so now, you're not just dealing with your own pain, but also worrying you'll be dismissed or misunderstood.
But here's something to pay attention to—doubt isn't the enemy of faith. In fact, it can be the doorway to something much deeper. So many people who've had profound encounters with God started off with serious skepticism. They questioned, challenged, and wrestled with their beliefs. They refused to settle for easy answers, and it was right there—in the struggle—that they found something real. Something they couldn't just explain away.
Let me share a couple of stories. There was a man who grew up in a totally secular home. After losing someone he loved, he started searching for meaning. He dove into philosophy, science, religion—you name it—but nothing filled the hunger he felt for truth. Only when he got honest about his doubts, and brought them into conversation with God, did something shift. It wasn't dramatic, but it was unmistakable—a sense of being seen and known, even while he was still confused.
Then there was a woman, burned out by years of religious hypocrisy. She left faith behind and built a life on reason and self-reliance. But that ache for something more just wouldn’t go away. In therapy, she began to name the wounds—how people, claiming to speak for God, had hurt her. Slowly, she found the courage to separate her painful experiences with religion from the possibility of a living God. Over time, her faith grew into something deeper and more genuine than she’d ever known.
These stories really highlight something important: faith isn't about having zero doubts. It's about moving forward, even when things aren't certain. It's a journey, not just a destination—a process of asking questions, searching, sometimes stumbling along the way. For a lot of people, the most powerful moments with God don't come from certainty, but from wrestling with questions that don’t have easy answers.
So, what does this mean in therapy? It means making space for doubt—not as a problem to fix, but as a vital part of the journey. It takes real courage to ask hard questions, and it’s important to resist the urge to just hand out quick fixes or easy platitudes. Sometimes, that means grappling with suffering—wondering how a loving God could allow so much pain. Sometimes, it means confronting the failures of religious communities and figuring out how to trust again.
What comes out of all this? A faith that's humble and resilient. It's not about blind acceptance or rigid rules—it's about lived experience. It's knowing you've encountered something real, even when you're still wrestling with doubts. And that kind of faith? It's not threatened by tough questions. If anything, it grows stronger—more authentic—with every challenge.
In a world obsessed with certainty and control, this journey can feel risky. But if you're willing to take that leap, the rewards are profound. You discover a God who welcomes your questions, who meets you right in the middle of your struggles. And you find a faith that's not just a set of beliefs, but a living relationship—one that brings hope, healing, and transformation in ways that you can't always explain.

Chapter Six: The Wounds We Carry—Healing from Spiritual Trauma.
You know, some of the deepest wounds we carry aren’t the ones you can see. They’re the hurts that settle quietly in your heart, shaped by years of disappointment, betrayal, or even outright harm by people who once claimed to speak for God. In a therapy room, these kinds of wounds often show up in surprising ways—maybe a sudden flinch when someone mentions prayer, or a tightness in your chest when you think about old church memories, or even a quiet anger that just won’t let go.
Let me share a story. There was a woman who still remembered, decades later, the sting of being shamed by a youth leader. She was told her questions were sinful, that her doubts meant her faith was weak. Over the years, she learned to hide her true self. Honesty, she thought, would only bring more rejection. So, in therapy, all that old pain came flooding back—mixed with a deep hope that maybe, just maybe, God could be different from the people who had hurt her.
Or take a man who grew up in a strict religious home. He described his childhood as one ruled by fear. Every mistake brought threats of divine punishment, and love always felt like it came with strings attached. As an adult, he found it hard to trust anyone—including God. The idea of grace? That felt almost dangerous, as if letting his guard down would only invite trouble.
These aren’t rare stories. Spiritual trauma can leave you feeling alone, ashamed, even cut off from the comfort you need most. The road to healing? It’s hardly ever a straight line. It often starts by simply naming the pain—giving voice to anger, grief, and confusion that’s been buried for years.
In the safe space of a therapy relationship, something starts to change. Old beliefs get gently questioned. Is God really as harsh as you were taught? Could it be that those who hurt you were just... wrong? Slowly, new ways of seeing start to appear. Some people find hope by reimagining God—not as a distant judge, but as a loving presence who actually grieves with them. Others discover their anger isn’t a wall between them and faith, but a sign of how deeply they long for justice and truth.
Healing from spiritual trauma is really about taking back your story. It’s learning to see the difference between what flawed humans have done, and who the Divine actually is. For many, this means a season of wrestling—questioning, doubting, maybe even stepping away from old beliefs for a while. But with time, a new kind of faith can take root. It’s quieter, humbler, and far more honest. It’s not shaped by fear anymore, but by the hard-earned belief that love is stronger than shame.
And it’s in those moments—the quiet, ordinary ones—that people often sense God’s presence the most. Not in big, dramatic gestures, but in the soft assurance that healing really is possible. The journey isn’t easy, but it’s real. And for anyone who’s been wounded by religion, discovering a God who’s gentle, patient, and kind can truly change everything.

Chapter 7: The Practice of Presence—Experiencing God in Daily Life.
You know, for a lot of people, the idea of actually experiencing God can feel way out of reach. Like it’s only possible for saints, mystics, or those with a rock-solid faith. But if you listen to the stories that unfold in the therapy room, something different comes to light. God’s presence isn’t locked away on mountaintops or hidden in dramatic miracles. More often, it shows up in the simple, ordinary rhythms that make up our daily lives.
Picture this: a mother, completely overwhelmed by work and family, finds herself folding laundry at the end of a long day. Suddenly, she’s wrapped in a quiet sense of peace. The chaos fades, and for just a moment, she feels held—like she isn’t alone after all. It wasn’t flashy or dramatic, but it was real. That was presence.
Or imagine a man, struggling with loneliness after a painful breakup. He starts noticing little moments of grace—a stranger’s kind word, the warmth of sunlight on his skin, the comfort of a favorite song on the radio. These moments don’t erase the pain. But they offer tiny glimpses of hope—a gentle sense that, even here, something good is still possible.
See, the practice of presence isn’t really about having the right technique. It’s more about being open—paying attention to the subtle ways God shows up. Sometimes it’s in beauty, sometimes in kindness, and sometimes in that still space between your thoughts. For some folks, that might mean prayer or meditation. For others, it could be a walk in nature, a moment with art, or even helping someone out.
There’s one woman who was pretty skeptical about religion. But she started practicing gratitude every evening, jotting down three things she was thankful for. At first, it was just an exercise. But over time, something shifted. She didn’t just feel better—she started noticing the sacred, quietly woven through her everyday life.
Here’s something to pay attention to: these practices aren’t about trying to earn God’s approval. They’re not about being perfect. It’s really just about making space for the possibility of encounter. Most of us don’t realize how easy it is to miss these moments. We get distracted by busyness, or weighed down by our worries. But when we slow down and pay attention, even the ordinary can suddenly feel meaningful.
In therapy, clients are often invited to experiment with these small practices. Not because they’re a magic fix, but as a gentle way to open up to God’s presence in their real, messy lives. And many people are surprised by what they find—a sense of peace, even when life is chaotic, a new way of seeing old problems, or a quiet joy that bubbles up for no obvious reason.
Over time, these little moments add up. They become the foundation for a faith that’s lived, not just believed. God’s presence stops being just an idea. It becomes something real—something you can lean on for comfort, guidance, and hope, no matter what you’re facing.

Chapter 8: The Courage to Surrender—Letting Go and Trusting the Unknown
There comes a point in every journey where the old ways just... stop working. You know how sometimes, the things you used to rely on—like control, avoiding tough feelings, or even denying what’s really going on—just start to crumble? For a lot of people, that’s the moment when everything changes.
Picture this: a father, worn down by years of trying to fix his family’s problems, finally admits he can’t do it on his own. The weight he’s been carrying is just too heavy. So, he drops to his knees and whispers a quiet prayer of surrender. And in that moment, something shifts. The problems don’t magically disappear, but suddenly, the burden feels a little lighter. He realizes—he doesn’t have to carry it all by himself.
Or think about a young woman, frozen by anxiety about what the future might hold. She’s planned out every detail, holding tight to the idea that if she controls everything, nothing will go wrong. But when life takes its own turn and her plans unravel, she’s forced to face her biggest fear—the unknown. In therapy, she starts to wonder: what if, instead of trying to predict every outcome, she could trust in something beyond herself? Not just her own plans, but the idea that she’s not alone on this path.
See, surrender isn’t about giving up, and it’s definitely not about just letting life happen to you. It’s an act of real courage. It’s about letting go of the need for certainty, and opening yourself to something bigger. And honestly, for most of us, that’s the hardest step. There’s this fear that if we let go, everything will come crashing down.
But here’s what’s amazing: when you listen to the stories of people who’ve actually taken that risk—who’ve dared to let go—a new pattern starts to appear. Letting go becomes this doorway to freedom. The grip of anxiety finally loosens. Relationships start to heal, often in ways no one expected. And suddenly, there’s room for new possibilities to take root.
Most of us don’t even realize how much energy we spend trying to control things we just can’t control. When you finally release that energy, you make space for something new and unexpected to enter your life.
If you look at surrender through the lens of faith, it’s really an invitation to trust—that even when you can’t see the outcome, there’s a goodness at the heart of things. It’s a leap into the unknown, but with this quiet assurance that love is what holds it all together.
Therapists see this transformation all the time. Clients who once felt trapped by fear or weighed down by shame begin to move through life with more freedom. They discover that being vulnerable isn’t a weakness—it’s actually a source of strength. The journey doesn’t magically get easier, but you’re no longer walking it alone.

Chapter 9: The Ripple Effect — How Personal Healing Transforms Communities.
Have you ever noticed how real healing just can’t help but spill over into the lives of others? When someone’s loneliness is finally met with love, or the heavy weight of shame is gently lifted by grace, it doesn’t just stay with them. That kind of change sends ripples—touching families, friendships, and entire communities.
Picture a mother, once weighed down by anxiety. Through her journey of faith and therapy, she finds new confidence and a sense of self-acceptance. Her children pick up on the difference almost right away. The house feels lighter; arguments fade, and suddenly, laughter fills the dinner table again. Her healing? It becomes a gift to everyone around her.
Or think about a man who’s been distant from his brother for years. It takes real courage, but he finally reaches out. Sure, the old wounds don’t disappear overnight, but forgiveness cracks the door open to something new. Soon, a family that was divided by bitterness starts to find its way back to each other.
Stories like these aren’t rare. Over and over, you’ll see how personal transformation changes relationships. People who’ve experienced grace become more gracious. Those who find hope? They become living, breathing sources of hope for others. The presence of God—first felt in the quiet of someone’s heart—begins to show up in small acts of kindness, patience, and generosity.
In therapy, people are often surprised by just how much their own healing affects those around them. Maybe it’s a woman who learns to set healthy boundaries, and suddenly her friendships feel deeper and more real. Or a man who faces his fears and discovers new opportunities—at work, in his community, everywhere.
The ripple effect isn’t always some big, dramatic moment. Sometimes, it’s as simple as a smile, a listening ear, or a word of encouragement. But over time, those small acts add up. They create a culture of compassion—where people feel seen, valued, and supported.
And for folks who’ve gone through spiritual healing, there’s often this natural pull to give back. Some become mentors or volunteers. Others step up as advocates for change. But a lot of people just live with greater kindness and integrity—letting their actions speak for themselves.
When individuals are transformed, communities start to change, too. The process might be slow, even quiet, but the impact is real and lasting. Most people don’t realize just how much difference one healed heart can make.
But listen to the stories shared in a therapy room, and it’s clear as day: when someone encounters the living God, the world around them starts to shift. That’s the power of the ripple effect.

Chapter 10: Living with Mystery—Embracing Uncertainty and Wonder
You know, it’s so natural to want certainty—to look for answers that explain everything and wrap up all the loose ends. But on this journey of faith and healing, certainty can feel almost out of reach.
The more we encounter the reality of God, the more we notice just how much we don’t know. And honestly, there’s something kind of beautiful about that.
Think about a scientist—someone who’s trained to rely on evidence and logic. She found herself facing questions that science just couldn’t touch. The birth of her child, the breathtaking colors of a sunset, that deep longing for something more—all these little moments pointed toward a reality that can’t be measured or explained away.
In therapy, she learned to make peace with not having all the answers. She started to welcome the wonder, and the mystery, that sits right at the heart of life.
And then there’s the man who’s been crushed by loss. He wrestled with the question—why does suffering exist? He searched everywhere for answers, but none of them felt complete. Over time, he realized he could actually live with the questions. He discovered he could carry both grief and hope, both doubt and faith, side by side in his heart.
Embracing mystery doesn’t mean giving up on understanding. It’s about recognizing our limits, and making space for awe. It’s letting go of the urge to control or explain every little thing, and instead, opening up to the idea that life is so much bigger, deeper, and more beautiful than we could ever imagine.
In therapy, it’s common for clients to be encouraged to sit with their questions—not to rush toward an answer, even when it feels uncomfortable or scary. And here’s something to really pay attention to: over time, this willingness to live with uncertainty is actually a sign of maturity, not weakness.
For many, this openness becomes a doorway to experiencing God in a new way—not as a puzzle to solve, but as a presence to encounter. The journey shifts; it’s less about reaching a destination, and more about walking forward with wonder, curiosity, and trust.

As we wrap up this journey together, I want you to take a deep breath and just let these thoughts sink in.
If you’ve been following along, you’ve probably noticed how the longing for something bigger—for God—really is woven through every part of life. This path isn’t always tidy or straightforward. There are questions, setbacks, moments that hurt, and moments that fill us with joy. But one thing keeps showing up: healing is possible, and this living, loving God is closer than we ever imagine.
So, what does this mean for you? Here are a few things I hope you remember:
That ache for purpose in your heart? It’s not a weakness—it’s a signpost, pointing you somewhere true.
Healing often begins when you have the courage to name your wounds, and invite God right into those tender places.
And faith doesn’t mean you never doubt. You can hold both faith and questions in your hands—because both are welcome on the journey.
Sometimes, it’s just a small act of being present, or letting go, that opens up the door to real transformation.
And when you start to heal, that change doesn’t stop with you. It radiates outward—touching your family, your friends, even your community.
You don’t have to have everything figured out to start. This path isn’t about getting it perfect—it’s about being open. Honest about where you are, brave enough to hope, and willing to trust you’re not walking alone.
If you’re carrying pain from the past, healing really is possible. If you wrestle with doubt, your questions are part of the journey. And if you find yourself longing for something more, know that the longing itself is an invitation.
These stories aren’t just about other people—they’re about all of us. Each of our journeys is unique, but the invitation is the same: open your heart to the possibility that a living, loving God wants to meet you, right where you are.
So, take that next step, no matter how small. Look for those little moments of grace in your day. Reach out for support if you need it. And above all, remember: the path to healing isn’t something you have to walk alone. There is a gentle, steady presence walking with you—offering hope, comfort, and the promise of new life.
